name: Proton pump inhibition
fields: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) on the luminal membrane of gastric parietal cells.
Irreversible blockade of the final common step of acid secretion — acid production stops regardless of what stimulated the pump (histamine, gastrin, or acetylcholine).

Because inhibition is irreversible, effect duration tracks pump turnover (~24–48h to regenerate meaningful capacity), not plasma half-life — this is why once-daily dosing works despite a short half-life. Activation requires the pump to be actively secreting acid, hence the meal-timing rule.
Omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole.
Blocking the shared final pathway is more complete than blocking any single upstream receptor — the reason PPIs outperform H2 blockers on acid suppression.

H2 receptor antagonists block only the histamine-driven input, leaving gastrin/acetylcholine-driven secretion untouched. PCABs (below) hit the identical target reversibly, without needing acid-catalyzed activation.

name: Potassium-competitive acid blockade
fields: The same H⁺/K⁺-ATPase as PPIs, but at the potassium-binding site rather than the covalent cysteine site PPIs use.
Reversible, competitive inhibition — the pump is blocked without needing chemical activation by stomach acid first.
Faster onset (no multi-dose ramp-up), no dependence on meal timing for activation, and more complete/consistent suppression, including overnight.
Removes the single biggest practical limitation of PPIs — the requirement for an acidic, meal-stimulated environment to switch on.
Faster and more genotype-independent than PPIs; still the same final target, so downstream physiology like rebound acid hypersecretion on withdrawal is relevant to both classes.

name: COX inhibition
fields: Cyclooxygenase enzymes — COX-1 (mostly constitutive) and COX-2 (mostly inducible) — which convert arachidonic acid into prostaglandins and thromboxane.
Reduced prostaglandin synthesis lowers inflammation, pain signaling, and fever — but also reduces gastroprotective/renal-protective prostaglandins (COX-1) and vascular prostacyclin (COX-2).

The same enzyme family explains the therapeutic effect and essentially all major NSAID toxicities at once — GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk are different faces of one mechanism, not separate side effects.
Ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac (nonselective); celecoxib, etoricoxib (COX-2 selective); aspirin (irreversible, uniquely antiplatelet).

A textbook case of one molecular target explaining an entire risk-benefit profile — see NSAID Evolution for how 40 years of drug design tried to split the "good" and "bad" effects of this one enzyme family.

Acetaminophen achieves analgesia/antipyresis through a still-debated, mostly central mechanism without meaningful peripheral COX-1/2 inhibition — explaining its GI safety and lack of real anti-inflammatory effect.

name: Cell wall synthesis inhibition
fields: Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) — enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan strands in the bacterial cell wall.
Without cross-linking, the wall can’t withstand osmotic pressure and the bacterium lyses — bactericidal, and selective for bacteria since human cells have no cell wall.
Time-dependent killing — efficacy tracks how long drug levels stay above the minimum inhibitory concentration, not how high the peak is — which drives beta-lactam dosing frequency.
One of the cleanest examples of selective toxicity in pharmacology: the target simply doesn’t exist in human cells.
Vancomycin (not covered elsewhere on this site) blocks an earlier step in the same broad pathway — useful against organisms resistant to PBP-targeting beta-lactams.

name: Protein synthesis inhibition — 30S subunit
fields: Tetracyclines block aminoacyl-tRNA binding (bacteriostatic); aminoglycosides cause misreading of the genetic code during translation (bactericidal) — same subunit, different binding site, different outcome.

Aminoglycoside uptake requires active oxidative bacterial metabolism, which is exactly why the class has zero activity against anaerobes — a direct mechanistic consequence, not a spectrum coincidence.
Shows that sharing a ribosomal subunit doesn’t mean sharing a mechanism or outcome — binding site and downstream consequence matter as much as target identity.
The 50S-targeting drugs below hit a different ribosomal component entirely, which is why tetracyclines and macrolides don’t share cross-resistance despite both inhibiting protein synthesis.

name: Protein synthesis inhibition — 50S subunit
fields: Macrolides block translocation during elongation; clindamycin binds an overlapping site with a similar effect — both mostly bacteriostatic.

Because macrolides and clindamycin share an overlapping binding site, ribosomal methylation resistance (the MLSb phenotype) confers cross-resistance across both — the basis for the clinical D-test before relying on clindamycin against certain staph isolates.

Explains both the shared toxin-suppression utility of this group (less protein synthesis means less bacterial exotoxin production, relevant in severe strep/staph disease) and the shared resistance liability.
Contrast with the 30S-targeting drugs above — different subunit, no cross-resistance, entirely different spectrum logic.

name: Folate synthesis inhibition
fields: Two sequential bacterial folate-synthesis enzymes — dihydropteroate synthase (blocked by sulfamethoxazole) and dihydrofolate reductase (blocked by trimethoprim).
Blocking two steps in the same pathway is synergistic — bacteria can’t easily route around a sequential double block the way they might a single-step inhibition.

Human cells obtain folate from the diet rather than synthesizing it — which is why this pathway is selectively bacterial, and why methotrexate (which blocks the analogous mammalian enzyme) is such a dangerous combination with trimethoprim.
A clean example of deliberate sequential blockade as a pharmacological strategy, distinct from simply combining two unrelated mechanisms.
Most other classes here hit a single, non-sequential target — this combination’s synergy is a designed feature, not a coincidence of co-administration.

name: DNA replication inhibition
fields: Bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV — enzymes that manage DNA supercoiling during replication.
Blocking these enzymes prevents DNA unwinding/religation, causing strand breaks and cell death — bactericidal, concentration-dependent.

Structural distinctness from human topoisomerases makes the class selectively bactericidal, though its broader connective-tissue adverse effects (tendon, CNS, vascular) remain an area of ongoing research rather than a fully settled mechanism.
Illustrates concentration-dependent killing — higher peak-to-MIC ratios predict efficacy, a genuinely different dosing philosophy than the time-dependent logic of beta-lactams.
Directly contrasts with beta-lactams’ time-dependent killing — two different bactericidal strategies requiring different dosing logic to optimize.

name: Keratinization normalization
fields: Normalizes the rate and pattern of keratinocyte shedding within the follicle, preventing the abnormal cohesion that forms a microcomedone — the first step of acne pathogenesis.

Because this addresses the earliest step in the pathogenic cascade, retinoids are foundational/first-line for comedonal acne — but the same turnover-acceleration is also what causes the initial "purge" and irritation.
A rare case where one receptor-mediated effect explains both a drug’s primary benefit and its main tolerability challenge.
Salicylic acid achieves a related but distinct outcome — direct chemical exfoliation of the follicular lining, without receptor signaling — part of why it’s gentler but generally less powerful.

name: Antimicrobial + anti-inflammatory dual mechanisms
fields: Varies by drug — tetracyclines act on the C. acnes 30S ribosome and, separately, inhibit matrix metalloproteinases and neutrophil chemotaxis; benzoyl peroxide combines non-specific oxidative bacterial killing with mild direct comedolytic activity.
Two mechanistically independent effects from one molecule — antibacterial and anti-inflammatory action don’t have to travel together, but in these specific agents, they do.

Explains why sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline is sometimes used purely for its anti-inflammatory effect, independent of any antibacterial goal, and why benzoyl peroxide stays useful even with sparse bacterial involvement.
Doxycycline/minocycline (dual mechanism in acne), benzoyl peroxide (oxidative kill + mild comedolytic).
A reminder that a drug’s effect in a specific indication isn’t always fully explained by its textbook primary mechanism.
Contrast with topical clindamycin, which is essentially single-mechanism (antibacterial only) here — part of why it’s paired with benzoyl peroxide for a complementary, not redundant, effect.
